claim: Activation-induced deaminase (AID) can drive lymphomagenesis by generating off-target DNA breaks at loci that harbor highly active enhancers and display convergent transcription.
source: Activation-induced deaminase (AID) can drive lymphomagenesis by generating off-target DNA breaks at loci that harbor highly active enhancers and display convergent transcription.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research establishing this mechanism.

claim: The first active transcriptional profiles from acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) patients acquired here reveal striking similarity at structural variation (SV) sites.
source: The first active transcriptional profiles from acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) patients acquired here reveal striking similarity at structural variation (SV) sites.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on GRO-seq data from ALL patients.

claim: Specific transcriptional features, namely convergent transcription and Pol2 stalling, were detected at breakpoints.
source: Specific transcriptional features, namely convergent transcription and Pol2 stalling, were detected at breakpoints.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on analysis of GRO-seq and ChIP-seq data.

claim: The overlap was most prominent at SV with recognition motifs for the recombination activating genes (RAG).
source: The overlap was most prominent at SV with recognition motifs for the recombination activating genes (RAG).
evidence: This finding is based on analysis of breakpoint data with RSS motifs.

claim: Convergent transcription contributes to R-loop generation and RNA polymerase stalling.
source: We present signal feature analysis to detect vulnerable regions and quantified from human cells how convergent transcription contributes to R-loop generation and RNA polymerase stalling.
evidence: This is demonstrated through DRIP-seq and GRO-seq analysis.

claim: Wide stalling regions were characterized by high DNAse hypersensitivity and unusually broad H3K4me3 signal.
source: Wide stalling regions were characterized by high DNAse hypersensitivity and unusually broad H3K4me3 signal.
evidence: This is based on analysis of DNAse-seq and ChIP-seq data.

claim: Based on 1382 pre-B-ALL patients, the ETV6-RUNX1 fusion positive patients had over ten-fold elevation in RAG1.
source: Based on 1382 pre-B-ALL patients, the ETV6-RUNX1 fusion positive patients had over ten-fold elevation in RAG1 while high expression of AID marked pre-B-ALL lacking common cytogenetic changes.
evidence: This is based on transcriptome analysis of 1382 pre-B-ALL patients.

claim: High expression of AID marked pre-B-ALL lacking common cytogenetic changes.
source: Based on 1382 pre-B-ALL patients, the ETV6-RUNX1 fusion positive patients had over ten-fold elevation in RAG1 while high expression of AID marked pre-B-ALL lacking common cytogenetic changes.
evidence: This is based on transcriptome analysis showing AICDA expression patterns.

claim: In precursor lymphoblastic leukemia, primary genetic lesions often arise in utero.
source: In precursor lymphoblastic leukemia, primary genetic lesions often arise in utero (Wiemels et al., 1999; Mori et al., 2002; Maia et al., 2003, Bateman et al., 2015), while the onset of overt disease requires additional genetic alterations.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The onset of overt disease requires additional genetic alterations.
source: In precursor lymphoblastic leukemia, primary genetic lesions often arise in utero (Wiemels et al., 1999; Mori et al., 2002; Maia et al., 2003, Bateman et al., 2015), while the onset of overt disease requires additional genetic alterations.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by citations.

claim: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) of ETV6-RUNX1 positive acute leukemias suggested that the secondary lesions are predominantly caused by off-target activity of the RAG complex.
source: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) of ETV6-RUNX1 (also known as TEL-AML1) positive acute leukemias suggested that the secondary lesions are predominantly caused by off-target activity of the RAG complex (Papaemmanuil et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on prior WGS study cited.

claim: The expression of the AID complex in more mature B cells is implicated in genomic instability and development of lymphomas.
source: In a similar fashion, the expression of the AID complex in more mature B cells is implicated in genomic instability and development of lymphomas (Meng et al., 2014; Qian et al., 2014; Robbiani et al. 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Antigen receptor genes are assembled from discrete gene segments by RAG-mediated V(D)J recombination at sites of recombination signal sequences (RSS) during early lymphocyte development.
source: Antigen receptor genes are assembled from discrete gene segments by RAG-mediated V(D)J recombination at sites of recombination signal sequences (RSS) during early lymphocyte development (Gellert 2002; Schatz and Swanson, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The expression of RAG1 and RAG2 is limited to precursor stages of lymphocytes.
source: Cells incorporate multiple strategies to control the action of the RAG complex to appropriate genomic loci: the expression of RAG1 and RAG2 is limited to precursor stages of lymphocytes, the activity of the complex is attenuated during S-phase of cell cycle, and RAG cleavage is directed towards RSS pair containing sequences (Schatz and Swanson, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The activity of the RAG complex is attenuated during S-phase of cell cycle.
source: Cells incorporate multiple strategies to control the action of the RAG complex to appropriate genomic loci: the expression of RAG1 and RAG2 is limited to precursor stages of lymphocytes, the activity of the complex is attenuated during S-phase of cell cycle, and RAG cleavage is directed towards RSS pair containing sequences (Schatz and Swanson, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: RAG cleavage is directed towards RSS pair containing sequences.
source: Cells incorporate multiple strategies to control the action of the RAG complex to appropriate genomic loci: the expression of RAG1 and RAG2 is limited to precursor stages of lymphocytes, the activity of the complex is attenuated during S-phase of cell cycle, and RAG cleavage is directed towards RSS pair containing sequences (Schatz and Swanson, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The engagement of RAG2 is further limited by the histone modification H3K4me3, which is typically found at transcription start sites (TSS).
source: The engagement of RAG2 is further limited by the histone modification H3K4me3, which is typically found at transcription start sites (TSS) (Matthews et al., 2007; Teng et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: RSS and RSS-like motifs are found only at around 7–40% of breakpoints at SV sites.
source: However, RSS and RSS-like motifs are found only at around 7–40% of breakpoints at SV (genomic imbalance, translocation or inversion) sites (Andersson et al., 2015; Papaemmanuil et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on prior WGS studies cited.

claim: RSS motifs and H3K4me3 occur frequently in the genome suggesting that additional features are relevant for the genetic instability underlying leukemia SV.
source: Furthermore, the RSS motifs and H3K4me3 occur frequently in the genome suggesting that additional features, possibly even additional complexes including AID (Swaminathan et al., 2015), are relevant for the genetic instability underlying leukemia SV.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that RSS and H3K4me3 are common but SV is specific.

claim: In lymphomas, AID off-target effects localize to intragenic super-enhancer (SE) and promoter areas characterized by transcription from both strands, i.e. convergent transcription (convT).
source: In lymphomas, AID off-target effects localize to intragenic super-enhancer (SE) and promoter areas characterized by transcription from both strands, i.e. convergent transcription (convT) (Meng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: VH gene segment recombination by RAG at the IgH locus coincides with sense- and antisense transcription.
source: Notably, VH gene segment recombination by RAG at the IgH locus coincides with sense- and antisense transcription (Bolland et al., 2004), which could be relevant also at off-target sites.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Stalled polymerases are found at exons, R-loops and actively paused at TSS regions.
source: Secondly, stalled polymerases, which are found at exons, R-loops and actively paused at TSS regions (Jonkers and Lis, 2015), expose single stranded DNA, recruiting AID via Spt5 binding (Pavri et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Stalled polymerases expose single stranded DNA, recruiting AID via Spt5 binding.
source: Secondly, stalled polymerases, which are found at exons, R-loops and actively paused at TSS regions (Jonkers and Lis, 2015), expose single stranded DNA, recruiting AID via Spt5 binding (Pavri et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The polymerase complex displaces nucleosomes completely or partially (the H2A/H2B moiety), which in vitro promotes cleavage by RAGs.
source: Furthermore, the polymerase complex displaces nucleosomes completely or partially (the H2A/H2B moiety), which in vitro promotes cleavage by RAGs (Bevington and Boyes, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: RNA polymerases engaged into primary transcription across the genome can be measured using Global-Run-On sequencing (GRO-seq).
source: RNA polymerases engaged into primary transcription across the genome can be measured using Global-Run-On sequencing (GRO-seq) (Kaikkonen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the GRO-seq method supported by citation.

claim: Transcriptional activity from ALL cells representing seven different pre-B-ALL cytogenetic subtypes was assayed using GRO-seq.
source: Transcriptional activity from ALL cells representing seven different pre-B-ALL cytogenetic subtypes was assayed using GRO-seq (both primary patient and cell line samples, see Supplementary file 1 and Materials and methods), and jointly analyzed with WGS data from the ETV6-RUNX1 (51 cases; Papaemmanuil et al., 2014), high hyperdiploid (HeH, 16 cases; Paulsson et al., 2015), hypodiploid (20 cases; Holmfeldt et al., 2013) and MLL-rearranged (22 cases at diagnosis and 2 relapses; Andersson et al., 2015) subtypes of precursor B-ALL.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach of the study.

claim: An increasing trend of transcriptional activity was observed when TADs were compared based on breakpoint frequency quartiles.
source: An increasing trend of transcriptional activity was observed when TADs were compared based on breakpoint frequency quartiles (see Materials and methods, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of transcription levels in TADs with different breakpoint frequencies.

claim: The PAX5 and ZCCHC7 genes are located within a TAD region with 20 breakpoints in the ETV6-RUNX1, 4 in HeH and 6 in MLL subtype.
source: The PAX5 and ZCCHC7 genes are located within a TAD region with 20 breakpoints in the ETV6-RUNX1, 4 in HeH and 6 in MLL subtype (excluding the MLL-fusion itself) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of breakpoint data in specific TADs.

claim: GRO-seq exhibited transcription signal spanning several hundred thousand base pairs in regions with no annotated coding genes, typical of long non-coding transcripts.
source: Frequent SV were also found in TADs with no annotated coding genes (Figure 1C, 20 breakp in ETV6-RUNX1; Figure 1D, 4 breakp in HeH), yet GRO-seq exhibited transcription signal spanning several hundred thousand base pairs in both regions, typical of long non-coding transcripts (Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on GRO-seq data showing transcription in regions without annotated genes.

claim: The nascent ALL transcriptomes reveal novel transcribed regions as recurrent SV-associated hotspots in the two most common ALL subtypes.
source: The nascent ALL transcriptomes thus reveal novel transcribed regions as recurrent SV-associated hotspots in the two most common ALL subtypes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the GRO-seq data analysis.

claim: The prevailing notion is that active transcription start sites (TSS) in pre-B cells are susceptible to RAG off-targeting due to the H3K4me3 chromatin mark.
source: The prevailing notion is that active transcription start sites (TSS) in pre-B cells are susceptible to RAG off-targeting due to the H3K4me3 chromatin mark (Matthews et al., 2007; Teng et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Recurrent breakpoints often lied several kb downstream of TSS and coincided with simultaneous transcription on both strands.
source: However, we noticed that the recurrent breakpoints often lied several kb downstream of TSS, as highlighted in Figure 1B and D (see inserts), and coincided with simultaneous transcription on both strands, ie. convT spanning a minimum of 100 bp.
evidence: This is based on analysis of breakpoint locations relative to TSS and convT regions.

claim: Many of these regions likely correspond to transcription from intragenic enhancers that generate enhancer RNAs (eRNA) that are typically a few kb in size.
source: In closer examination of the signal data from leukemia SV hotspots, many of these regions likely correspond to transcription from intragenic enhancers that generate enhancer RNAs (eRNA) that are typically a few kb in size (Kaikkonen et al. 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the characteristics of the transcription signal and citation to prior research on eRNAs.

claim: A significant enrichment of breakpoints in enhancers overlapping with convT was observed.
source: In agreement, a significant enrichment of breakpoints in enhancers overlapping with convT was observed (hypergeometric test P=0.00012 for intergenic and P=4.6e-08 for all enhancers identified based on eRNA signal, see Materials and methods and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of breakpoint overlap with enhancers.

claim: An overlapping eRNA transcript at the TSS region of PAX5, confirmed by the active enhancer chromatin marker H3K27ac, led to convT extending nearly 20 kb, with SV sites located between 3.7–9.7 kb downstream of the TSS.
source: An overlapping eRNA transcript at the TSS region of PAX5, confirmed by the active enhancer chromatin marker H3K27ac, led to convT extending nearly 20 kb, with SV sites located between 3.7–9.7 kb downstream of the TSS (Figure 1B, see insert).
evidence: This is based on analysis of GRO-seq and ChIP-seq data at the PAX5 locus.

claim: ConvT in the vicinity of intragenic breakpoints was often associated with localized elevation in the GRO-seq signal.
source: Secondly, convT in the vicinity of intragenic breakpoints was often associated with localized elevation in the GRO-seq signal, as exemplified at the ZCCHC7 and RAG loci (Figure 2A, see also Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on observation of GRO-seq signal patterns at breakpoint sites.

claim: The observed signal features were highly reproducible between biological replicates and shared among a subset of cytogenetic groups.
source: The observed signal features were highly reproducible between biological replicates and shared among a subset of cytogenetic groups (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on comparison of replicate GRO-seq experiments.

claim: The signal features represent RNA polymerase II (Pol2) stalling events.
source: We hypothesized that they represent RNA polymerase II (Pol2) stalling events.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed signal patterns.

claim: Genome-wide analysis of convT and Pol2 stalling substantiated the relevance of these observations: considering the breakpoint frequency per TAD size, the top ranked TADs in each ALL subtype represented genomic regions with abundant convT and Pol2 stalling.
source: Genome-wide analysis of convT and Pol2 stalling (see Materials and methods and Figure 2—source data 1) substantiated the relevance of these observations: considering the breakpoint frequency per TAD size, the top ranked TADs in each ALL subtype represented genomic regions with abundant convT and Pol2 stalling (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on genome-wide analysis of transcriptional features and breakpoint data.

claim: Significant enrichment was confirmed for the upper quartiles (hypergeometric test P=0.00038 in ETV6-RUNX1, P=0.00018 in hyperdiploid, P=0.028 in hypodiploid and P=0.00004 in MLL-rearranged).
source: Significant enrichment was confirmed for the upper quartiles (hypergeometric test P=0.00038 in ETV6-RUNX1, P=0.00018 in hyperdiploid, P=0.028 in hypodiploid and P=0.00004 in MLL-rearranged).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the overlap between breakpoints and transcriptional features.

claim: The increased overlap was found for breakpoints with and without RSS motifs.
source: The increased overlap was found for breakpoints with and without RSS motifs (denoted as R-breakp and NR-breakp, see Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Materials and methods) and it was preserved when total transcriptional activity was considered (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on analysis of breakpoints categorized by RSS motif status.

claim: The distinct transcriptional profile of embryonic stem cells (ES) had lower overlap.
source: Furthermore, the distinct transcriptional profile of embryonic stem cells (ES) had lower overlap (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is based on analysis of ES cell GRO-seq data as a control.

claim: TADs with high number of breakpoints consistently had significant overlap with chromatin segments representing active transcription.
source: For comparison, chromatin segmentation of B-lymphoid cells was similarly analyzed (see Figure 1—source data 1 and Figure 2—source data 1). TADs with high number of breakpoints consistently had significant overlap with chromatin segments representing active transcription (refer to Figure 2—source data 1), supporting a transcription-coupled mechanism for the observed genetic instability.
evidence: This is based on analysis of chromatin segmentation data.

claim: RNA polymerases are expected to stall at regions harboring R-loop forming sequences (RLFS).
source: RNA polymerases are expected to stall at regions harboring R-loop forming sequences (RLFS) (Skourti-Stathaki et al., 2014a; Jenjaroenpun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: RLFS motif containing regions exhibited a significantly higher overlap with Pol2 stalling sites when compared to random intragenic regions.
source: These RLFS motif containing regions exhibited a significantly higher overlap with Pol2 stalling sites when compared to random intragenic regions (Figure 3B, empirical P<0.001 in B-lineage and ES cells).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of RLFS motifs and Pol2 stalling sites.

claim: A highly concordant local RLFS motif density and GRO-seq signal profile was observed across gene regions.
source: A highly concordant local RLFS motif density and GRO-seq signal profile was observed across gene regions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is based on comparison of RLFS motif density and GRO-seq signal.

claim: The profiles peaked near TSS, where the presence of RLFS motifs led to a significant elevation in the median GRO-seq signal level (2.1-fold increase in B-lineage cells, Wilcoxon rank sum test P<2.2e-16, 95% CI 2.1–2.3).
source: The profiles peaked near TSS, where the presence of RLFS motifs led to a significant elevation in the median GRO-seq signal level (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, 2.1-fold increase in B-lineage cells, Wilcoxon rank sum test P<2.2e-16, 95% CI 2.1–2.3).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of GRO-seq signal at TSS with and without RLFS motifs.

claim: Collisions due to convT may halt transcription in a dynamic and cell-specific manner.
source: As a second mechanism, collisions due to convT may halt transcription (Prescott and Proudfoot, 2002) in a dynamic and cell-specific manner.
evidence: This is based on prior research cited and inference about the mechanism.

claim: Higher antisense signal at convT regions increased the overlap with Pol2 stalling sites on the sense strand.
source: Accordingly, higher antisense signal at convT regions (see Materials and methods) increased the overlap with Pol2 stalling sites on the sense strand (Figure 3B), intriguingly exceeding that observed for RLFS motifs (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of antisense transcription levels and Pol2 stalling.

claim: DRIP-seq quantification showed 2.1-fold elevation in median signal confirmed that RLFS motifs favor DNA-RNA hybrid formation.
source: The 2.1-fold elevation in median DRIP-seq signal confirmed that RLFS motifs favor DNA-RNA hybrid formation (Figure 3C, Wilcoxon rank sum test P<2.2e-16, 95% CI 2.0–2.1, see Figure 3—source data 2 for each replicate).
evidence: This is based on DRIP-seq data analysis comparing regions with and without RLFS motifs.

claim: DRIP-seq quantification showed 1.7-fold higher median signal at convT-positive TSS regions.
source: Moreover, DRIP-seq quantification showed 1.7-fold higher median signal at convT-positive TSS regions (Figure 3D, Wilcoxon rank sum test P<2.2e-16, 95% CI 1.6–1.7).
evidence: This is based on DRIP-seq data analysis comparing TSS with and without convT.

claim: Transcription stalling occurs at RLFS and convT regions in mammalian cells that associates with R-loop formation based on evidence from ES cells.
source: These results demonstrate that transcription stalling occurs at RLFS and convT regions in mammalian cells that associates with R-loop formation based on evidence from ES cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the DRIP-seq and GRO-seq data analysis.

claim: A mechanistic link between R-loops and AID off-targeting has been established in lymphomas.
source: A mechanistic link between R-loops and AID off-targeting has been established in lymphomas (Alt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Significant genome-wide enrichment of breakpoints with the investigated transcriptional features was observed (29% overlap with Pol2 stalling within gene regions, binomial test P=4.088e-07; 9% genome-wide overlap with convT, P=5.16e-07).
source: We observed significant genome-wide enrichment of breakpoints with the investigated transcriptional features (Figure 3E and F, 29% overlap with Pol2 stalling within gene regions, binomial test P=4.088e-07; 9% genome-wide overlap with convT, P=5.16e-07).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of breakpoint overlap with transcriptional features.

claim: This enrichment of breakpoints to convT and Pol2 stalling regions was significant across a wide range of transcriptional activity.
source: This enrichment of breakpoints to convT and Pol2 stalling regions was significant across a wide range of transcriptional activity (refer to Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of breakpoints in genes binned by expression level.

claim: Breakpoint recurrence was found to increase the overlap with both Pol2 stalling and convT.
source: Co-occurrence of breakpoints within a 1-kb window was used to distinguish non-recurrent (one breakpoint) and recurrent (more than one breakpoint) events (Figure 3—source data 1). Breakpoint recurrence was found to increase the overlap with both Pol2 stalling (Figure 3E)and convT (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is based on analysis of recurrent versus non-recurrent breakpoints.

claim: The breakpoints in Pol2 stalling sites were concordant with analysis using Pol2 ChIP-seq (by 78%) and they co-localized with both Ser2 and Ser5 phosphorylated forms of Pol2 complex.
source: The breakpoints in Pol2 stalling sites were concordant with analysis using Pol2 ChIP-seq (by 78%) and they co-localized with both Ser2 and Ser5 phosphorylated forms of Pol2 complex (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on comparison of GRO-seq and ChIP-seq data.

claim: Locally depleted nucleosomes around the Pol2 complex may enhance access to RSS/RSS-like sequences.
source: Next, we focused on deciphering whether the transcriptional features associate with RAG off-targeting. We hypothesized that locally depleted nucleosomes around the Pol2 complex (Bevington and Boyes, 2013) may enhance access to RSS/RSS-like sequences.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on prior research cited.

claim: DNAse-seq signal peaks were significantly wider when overlapping with Pol2 stalling sites.
source: DNAse-seq signal peaks were significantly wider when overlapping with Pol2 stalling sites (Figure 4A). A 876 bp (95% CI, 855–896) increase was observed in B-lymphoblastoid cells and 412 bp (95% CI, 395–429) in ES cells (Wilcoxon rank sum test P<2.2e-16 in both cell types, see also Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of DNAse-seq peak widths.

claim: Pol2 stalling sites at TSS with RSS motifs were significantly wider than at other TSS, with a difference of 259 bp (95% CI, 79–475 bp, Wilcoxon rank sum test P=0.0024).
source: We selected TSS regions with RSS motifs for closer examination and found that Pol2 stalling sites at these TSS were significantly wider than at other TSS (Figure 4B), with a difference of 259 bp (95% CI, 79–475 bp, Wilcoxon rank sum test P=0.0024).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of Pol2 stalling width at TSS with RSS motifs.

claim: Wide Pol2 stalling increases the likelihood of RSS motif occurrence in accessible chromatin.
source: Thus, wide Pol2 stalling increases the likelihood of RSS motif occurrence in accessible chromatin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Pol2 stalling is wider at TSS with RSS motifs.

claim: The width of stalling did not correlate positively (Pearson's correlation −0.11; 95% CI, −0.09 to −0.13) with the transcription level of the corresponding gene, indicating that stalling events, and not just active transcription, are important.
source: The width of stalling did not correlate positively (Pearson's correlation −0.11; 95% CI, −0.09 to −0.13) with the transcription level of the corresponding gene, indicating that stalling events, and not just active transcription, are important.
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of stalling width and gene expression.

claim: Pol2 S5P, DNAse-seq and H3K4me3 peaks had highest odds ratio for overlap with the widest Pol2 stalling regions based on both B-lineage and ES cell data.
source: We further analyzed the top 5% of widest Pol2 stalling regions by comparing them to widest peaks from DNAse hypersensitivity and ChIP for histone marks (see Materials and methods). The odds ratios for the overlap are visualized as a heatmap (see Figure 4C, OR>10 is shown in darkest color tone, refer to Figure 4—source data 1 for more statistics). In addition to DNAse-seq and Pol2 ChIP peaks, the H3K4me3 was found among the top category, confirmed also by ChIP-seq data acquired from REH and Nalm6 cells (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of overlap between widest Pol2 stalling regions and various ChIP-seq/DNAse-seq peaks.

claim: The ETV6-RUNX1 R-breakp (335; 156 intragenic) had a 66% overlap with Pol2 stalling at intragenic regions (binomial test P<2.2e-16) and a 44% genome-wide overlap with convT (binomial test P<2.2e-16).
source: Next, the ETV6-RUNX1 R-breakp (335; 156 intragenic) were analysed for the genome-wide overlap with the transcriptional features. A 66% overlap was found with Pol2 stalling at intragenic regions (binomial test P<2.2e-16) and a 44% genome-wide overlap with convT (binomial test P<2.2e-16, see also Figure 3—source data 1 for joint analysis across pre-B-ALL subtypes).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of R-breakp overlap with transcriptional features.

claim: The overlap with Pol2 stalling had high agreement between GRO-seq and ChIP-seq and it increased at recurrent R-breakp.
source: The overlap with Pol2 stalling had high agreement between GRO-seq and ChIP-seq (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and it increased at recurrent R-breakp (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on comparison of GRO-seq and ChIP-seq data and analysis of recurrent breakpoints.

claim: Overlap with convT was considerable (91%) at regions with 4 or more breakpoints.
source: In addition, overlap with convT (Figure 4E) was considerable (91%) at regions with 4 or more breakpoints.
evidence: This is based on analysis of highly recurrent breakpoint regions.

claim: Regions with RLFS motifs or annotated TSSs showed less marked enrichment (up to 36%).
source: In comparison, regions with RLFS motifs or annotated TSSs showed less marked enrichment (up to 36%) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on comparison of overlap percentages for different features.

claim: The significant overlap with transcriptional features was preserved at a wide range of expression levels.
source: Similar, as for NR-breakp, the significant overlap with transcriptional features was preserved at a wide range of expression levels (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of breakpoints in genes binned by expression level.

claim: The presence of both convT and Pol2 stalling best characterized the recurrent ETV6-RUNX1 breakpoints with RSS motifs (101/148; compared to 20/70 without motif), with 90% (43/48, empirical P=0.002) co-occurrence at intragenic sites.
source: Overall, the presence of both convT and Pol2 stalling best characterized the recurrent ETV6-RUNX1 breakpoints with RSS motifs (101/148; compared to 20/70 without motif), with 90% (43/48, empirical P=0.002) co-occurrence at intragenic sites (see also Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is based on analysis of co-occurrence of transcriptional features at breakpoints.

claim: Among samples with annotation of cytogenetic subtype (N = 1008), the ETV6-RUNX1 cases (N = 153) exhibited 10.8-fold higher median level of RAG1 expression relative to other cases with annotated cytogenetic type (Wilcoxon rank sum test P<2.2e-16, 95% CI 8.6–13.6-fold).
source: Among samples with annotation of cytogenetic subtype (N = 1008), the ETV6-RUNX1 cases (N = 153) exhibited 10.8-fold higher median level of RAG1 expression relative to other cases with annotated cytogenetic type (Wilcoxon rank sum test P<2.2e-16, 95% CI 8.6–13.6-fold, Figure 5A) and also high RAG2 expression (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on transcriptome analysis of 1382 pre-B-ALL patients.

claim: AICDA expression was highest in the 'other' group (N = 267) that does not carry recurrent fusion genes or karyotypic changes.
source: Moreover, AICDA expression was also detected in a specific subset of patients. It was highest in the 'other' group (N = 267) that does not carry recurrent fusion genes or karyotypic changes (Figure 5C, no statistical evaluation was performed as majority of signal values were below detection level of 4.2 in log2 scale).
evidence: This is based on transcriptome analysis showing AICDA expression patterns.

claim: High levels of AICDA expression were particularly prevalent in sample clusters that corresponded to high risk cases from two independent ALL datasets (hypergeometric test P=7.19e-47).
source: Upon further examination, high levels of AICDA expression were particularly prevalent in sample clusters that corresponded to high risk cases from two independent ALL datasets (hypergeometric test P=7.19e-47, Figure 5H, see Supplementary file 5 for patient characteristics).
evidence: This is based on analysis of AICDA expression in high-risk patient samples.

claim: The highest level of AICDA expression was presented by a relapsed ALL case, and the RAG1 and RAG2 expression levels were 3.09- and 1.93-fold increased at relapse, respectively.
source: The highest level of AICDA expression was presented by a relapsed ALL case, and the RAG1 and RAG2 expression levels were 3.09- and 1.93-fold increased at relapse, respectively.
evidence: This is based on comparison of gene expression at diagnosis and relapse.

claim: The expression of AID and RAG is distinct in leukemia subtypes and clinical prognosis groups.
source: Based on the integrated patient profiles, the expression of AID and RAG is distinct in leukemia subtypes and clinical prognosis groups.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the transcriptome analysis.

claim: Pol2 stalling and convT strongly associate with recurrent breakpoint sites across the genome and at gene loci implicated in leukemia such as CDKN2A and PAX5.
source: Pol2 stalling and convT strongly associate with recurrent breakpoint sites across the genome and at gene loci implicated in leukemia such as CDKN2A and PAX5 (Sulong et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings with citation to prior research on these loci.

claim: The integrative analysis identified several putative long non-coding RNAs and eRNAs, which merit further investigation.
source: While protein-coding secondary hits required in disease progression have been recognized for some time, our integrative analysis identified several putative long non-coding RNAs and eRNAs, which merit further investigation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the GRO-seq data analysis.

claim: Earlier work has linked eRNAs generated from intragenic superenhancers with AID-mediated instability in lymphomas, proposing that convT leads to arrested transcription, in agreement with experimental evidence from yeast cells.

evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on DRIP-seq and GRO-seq data.

claim: These mechanisms of transcription-coupled genetic instability, earlier implicated in lymphomas and breast cancer, have relevance in multiple different cancer types.
